name: Michael Heseltine
role: British former deputy prime minister and Conservative cabinet minister
summary: Heseltine combines support for private enterprise and privatization with an active government industrial strategy and devolved economic development. He advocates European integration, NATO and a British nuclear deterrent; on free votes he consistently opposed the death penalty, backed legal abortion up to 24 weeks and let same-sex marriage proceed, while keeping a higher homosexual age of consent.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: As a backbencher in 1986 he voted for the Wages Bill cutting back the wages councils that set statutory minimum pay, and in 1992 for the bill abolishing them altogether.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He defends private enterprise and competition while identifying indispensable government functions.

public-ownership.rationale: As President of the Board of Trade he decided to privatise the modern nuclear power stations (1995), and as Defence Secretary he took the Royal Dockyards out of direct state management under commercial operators (1985).

reviewHistory.rationale: He defends electricity privatization and announces the transfer of modern nuclear generators into private ownership.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Opposed Labour's higher top-rate plans, said talking about taxing the rich would not help the economy, and criticised capital transfer tax as deterring job creation.

unions-good.rationale: Described union power as a source of strikes, restrictive practices and producer capture, said unions should not regain privileges, and praised Conservative union reform.

property-fundamental.rationale: Mixed: attacked the Community Land Act and confiscatory land powers, yet used compulsory acquisition powers for development corporations.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Mixed: said unfettered markets need government environmental regulation and defended regulation as protecting civilised life, but led the 1990s deregulation drive and called many regulations burdensome.

strong-leader.rationale: Criticised cabinet rubber-stamping and the closing of Parliament, called the Prime Minister first among equals; resigned from Cabinet in 1986 and challenged Thatcher in 1990.

state-harmful.rationale: He argues some economic tasks can only be performed by government.

limit-guns.rationale: He voted for government amendments widening the 1988 ban on self-loading rifles after Hungerford, but in 1997 voted against Labour's bill extending the handgun ban to .22 pistols, so he backed strict limits short of a total ban.

empower-police-military.rationale: He defends increasing defense resources and criticizes proposed spending reductions.

decide-locally.rationale: He proposes devolving growth budgets into locally controlled funding pots.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: In 2013 he voted Not Content on Lord Dear's motion to deny the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Bill a second reading, letting the bill proceed; his earlier doubts about its timing were words and give way to the vote.

reviewHistory.rationale: In 2013 he questioned the point and timing of legalizing same-sex marriage; this is qualified skepticism, not an explicit categorical ban.

reduce-immigration.rationale: His votes point both ways: in 1968 he was one of 62 MPs voting against the Commonwealth Immigrants Bill's restrictions, but as a backbencher in 1987 he voted for the Immigration Bill tightening control.

reviewHistory.rationale: Mixed: said immigration on too high a scale tests public acceptance and backed tighter laws under the Coalition, but also criticised the Home Secretary's clampdown and voted against the 1968 Commonwealth Immigration Bill.

free-trade.rationale: He endorses openness to trade and investment while reserving strategic safeguards.

nation-first.rationale: Held that Britain's self-interest lies in shared sovereignty and said standing isolationist as a lone nation state is unreal.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: He calls abandoning climate targets irresponsible even when action carries costs.

expand-nuclear.rationale: He supports continuing nuclear generation but rejects government finance for new plants, leaving expansion to commercial viability.

central-planning.rationale: His model partners with autonomous businesses rather than substituting comprehensive state planning.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Criticised capital transfer tax as a disincentive to create jobs and businesses, and credited cuts in inheritance tax with leaving wealth in the hands of people prepared to invest.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: His open-economy approach opposes general protectionism, allowing targeted national-interest intervention.

state-directs-investment.rationale: He advocates government industrial strategy, sector partnerships and coordinated investment.

widespread-small-property.rationale: He defends home ownership as a way to spread wealth and independence throughout society.

direct-votes.rationale: Mixed: proposed local polls on council spending in 1981 and backed a second Brexit referendum, but called mayoral referendums a disaster and opposed referendums on the euro and EU membership while a minister.

military-superiority.rationale: In 1985 set out the Western aim as maintaining balance, not achieving superiority.

results-over-ideology.rationale: He recounts making regeneration assistance conditional on party doctrine not obstructing a workable solution.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Called mandatory worker representation on company boards a disaster to be fought in the EC social charter, preferring wider share ownership.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: His 1992 motion rejected Opposition policies that would bring greater public borrowing, higher taxation and higher interest rates, and he stressed the need to tackle inflation first.

class-collaboration.rationale: Called for genuine partnerships between managers and employees (Investors in People) as the route to better industrial relations.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: He approved major coal-output contraction on market grounds; this does not establish opposition to every fossil fuel.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He explicitly gives government essential public-service and economic-development roles.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: As Environment Secretary he introduced and moved the 1980 Housing Bill that gave council tenants the statutory right to buy their homes.

reviewHistory.rationale: He introduced legislation establishing council tenants’ purchase rights.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Defended the Conservative trade union legislation as the basis of the best industrial relations in a century and attacked Labour's pledge to repeal it all.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: His words point both ways: after the 1981 riots he said tension tends to arise where different races live together, but in 2012 evidence to MPs he called the fast-growing ethnic diversity of London and Birmingham a huge potential strength to embrace.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: He explicitly confirms Britain’s commitment to an independent nuclear deterrent.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Proposed that the Bank of England be distanced from government on the Bundesbank model, with price stability as the overriding priority.

collective-defense.rationale: He presents nuclear deterrence as protection against attack on the Western Alliance.

common-currency.rationale: Welcomed the Government's move toward joining a successful single currency and urged an all-party campaign to lead opinion; earlier backed the ERM and Bundesbank-style discipline.

no-bailouts.rationale: As President of the Board of Trade in 1993 he refused to bail out Leyland DAF with taxpayers' money after its receivership, leaving receivers and banks to find a commercial rescue.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He voted against the 1999 House of Lords Bill removing hereditary peers, and in 2025 voted for ending hereditary by-elections rather than removing the sitting hereditary peers.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: He recalled in the Lords that he rebelled against his party when it wanted to resist the 1976 race relations legislation banning discrimination, and that the party changed its mind.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Insisted that power in the country rests in Parliament, called Parliament the ultimate custodian of national sovereignty, and said central government's mandate is exercised through the House.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Recommendation 73 supports using takeover powers to discourage unwanted strategic acquisitions in exceptional cases.

national-law-over-international.rationale: In 2020 he voted for Lord Judge's motion regretting that the Internal Market Bill would let ministers override the Withdrawal Agreement in breach of international law and the rule of law.

reviewHistory.rationale: He opposes unilateral withdrawal from the European human-rights convention and court, favoring negotiated reform.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: His votes point both ways: in 1982 he voted to decriminalise homosexual acts between consenting men over 21 in Northern Ireland, but in 1994 he voted against lowering the age of consent from 21 to 18 and in 2000 against equalising it at 16, keeping such acts between adults aged 18-20 criminal.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: He calls defense the government’s first responsibility and insists on funding the forces.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Defended Britain's place in the NATO alliance against the Soviet bloc and criticised unilateralists.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: He voted for the 1982 Northern Ireland Bill, which offered devolved government only on proposals commanding cross-community support rather than simple majority rule.

rent-control.rationale: Wanted rent deregulation through short-hold tenancies to bring back a market in private renting, as part of his critique of Labour housing policy.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: He supports maintaining and modernizing Britain’s own nuclear forces.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Defended hosting US-owned cruise missiles at RAF Greenham Common under existing Anglo-US arrangements.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Strongly backed water privatisation and attacked Labour's plan to renationalise water; no evidence he wanted hospitals or buses privatised.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Backed using force, within UN resolution 661, to reverse Iraq's occupation of Kuwait, a war not fought to defend Britain.

free-public-college.rationale: Voted Not Content on the Lords amendment (Triesman, December 2010) challenging the higher education fee regulations, so he let the raised fees stand; his own words are not on record.

pollution-taxes.rationale: He defends existing climate policy against proposals to scrap carbon taxes.

future-generations.rationale: Introducing the 1981 Wildlife and Countryside Bill he called conservation wise husbandry for the survival of our children and of generations yet to come, even at the cost of some immediate return.

arms-reduction.rationale: Backed NATO's twin-track policy: negotiated, verifiable reductions (zero option) alongside deployment, noting warhead numbers falling to a 20-year low.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: He defends retaining deterrence, allowing fewer warheads if the strategic situation changes substantially.

price-stability-first.rationale: He urged an independent Bank of England on the Bundesbank model, saying its anti-inflation disciplines are those all are committed to, and in 1993 restated the aim of price stability alongside firm control of public spending.

restrict-technology-exports-to-rivals.rationale: After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan he said exports that could enhance Soviet military power would be a concern and offered to review the COCOM export-control rules with allies.

avoid-permanent-military-alliances.rationale: He defended Britain's NATO membership and the credibility of its alliance commitments throughout his time as Defence Secretary.

notes:
Reviewed whole career: Right to Buy, defense and NATO, Westland/European industrial cooperation, coal closures, nuclear privatization, local regeneration, 2012 economic review, later Brexit opposition and 2025–26 statements. Downloaded and searched the full growth review across all themes, then reviewed every remaining null against the complete statement list. Rejoining the EU does not imply abolition of all borders; rejecting anti-asylum rhetoric does not establish a total immigration-number target. Nuclear generation is a mixed position: continued commercial operation supported, new state-financed plants rejected. His 2013 marriage comments question priority and timing, so confidence is low. Mine closures were not claimed as climate policy. No inferences from Conservative affiliation, cabinet colleagues’ statements, aristocratic title or personal gardening interests. Most penal, family, religious and digital-rights policies remain unknown.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 26 answers taken from it, 23 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Second independent pass built mainly from his own Commons speeches 1974-1999 (historic Hansard), his Lords speeches 2012-2024 (Hansard API) and his Lords division record. His memoirs and books (Life in the Jungle, The Challenge of Europe) are lending-only at the Internet Archive and could not be read. Where a vote or a minister's statement of government policy was the only evidence it is marked medium or low. Brexit-era answers rest on Lords speeches. No inferences from party or cabinet colleagues.

claude-opus-5-5 pass (2026-11-07, rules 5): brought the file to rules 4/5 (every source tagged action or words; answers on a record now cite the record alone). New sources: his Commons division record 1966-2001, read from the division lists in the local TheyWorkForYou Hansard copy and checked against the historic Hansard pages (death penalty, homosexual offences and age of consent, abortion, firearms, House of Lords Bill, Northern Ireland, Wages Bill, TURER, immigration bills); Lords divisions from the Lords Votes API (same-sex marriage 2013, Internal Market Bill 2020, hereditary peers 2025); his Commons speeches searched by theme (minimum wage, bail-outs, race, conservation, Soviet Union, export controls, price stability); the two maintainer-supplied texts (the 2012 growth review, already s1, and his 2012-13 oral evidence on it, HC 823). Changed: death-penalty (Wikipedia-only answer replaced by his free votes), same-sex-marriage (2013 vote overrides earlier words), right-to-buy, public-ownership, reduce-immigration, mixed-public-service-providers and national-law-over-international (re-sourced to actions alone). Searched without a usable position: proportional representation, Iraq 2003, assisted dying, China ties, Bosnia/Kosovo, aid, devolution to Scotland, freedom of information. Many society, religion and culture statements remain unrecorded.
